title: The Ultimate Joker Twist: Why Fans Want a Former Batman to Voice 'Absolute' Joker
summary:
Comic book fans are buzzing with a deliciously twisted idea: what if a former Batman actor voiced the Joker? Not just any Joker, but the 'Absolute' Joker from Scott Snyder's hit series, which flips the classic dynamic on its head. In this universe, Bruce Wayne is a young, trash-talking brawler—a far cry from the stoic Dark Knight—while Jack Grimm, the Joker, is an old-money billionaire with a secret cave and a squad of proteges. It's a complete role reversal, and fans think the metatextual casting would be chef's kiss.

With the 'Absolute Batman' animated series in development, fancasting has exploded. For Batman, names like Aleks Le—who recorded a fan-dub of a scene—and Roger Craig Smith are popular. But the Joker casting is where things get meta. Reddit user @MurdocksMother captured it perfectly: 'How funny would it be if they hired a previous Batman voice actor to play Absolute Joker?'

The idea isn't new; before the animated announcement, live-action fancasts included Christian Bale and Ben Affleck. Bale, in particular, stands out. His performance as Patrick Bateman in 'American Psycho'—a soulless businessman with a violent secret life—is essentially a Joker audition. Mix that with the intensity of his Batman, and you have the perfect unsettling blend. Hearing the hero of the 'Dark Knight' trilogy as a villain would be brilliantly disorienting.

Of course, landing a movie star for an ongoing series is a long shot. A more realistic option is Troy Baker, who has voiced both Batman and the Joker in various media. While it lacks the 'wow' factor, it carries the same symbolic weight: this Joker is essentially Bruce Wayne's dark mirror. Whether it's Bale or Baker, the casting choice could add a layer of meaning that makes this adaptation truly special.
why_it_matters: When you see how fans connect the dots between an actor's past roles and a story's themes, it shows that being creative isn't just for professionals — your own clever ideas can become part of a bigger cultural conversation, and sometimes even influence what gets made.

background_read: The idea of having a former Batman actor voice the Joker plays with a concept called 'metatextual' storytelling — where a story refers to itself or its own creation. For example, when an actor famously known as a hero takes on a villain role, it makes viewers think about how opposite those two characters are, even though they share a universe.

The 'Absolute Universe' is a recent line of comics from DC (the publisher of Batman and Superman) that reimagines classic heroes in new, often darker ways, written by Scott Snyder (a popular comic book writer who has won awards for his Batman stories).

Voice actors like Troy Baker (who has played both Batman and the Joker in video games and animated shows) are highly respected, but fans often dream of movie stars like Christian Bale — the actor who played Batman in Christopher Nolan's 'Dark Knight' films.
This type of fancasting spreads quickly on social media and sometimes even influences real casting decisions, showing how powerful fan creativity can be in shaping pop culture.

perspectives.description: The metatextual casting is seen as 'chef's kiss' — a perfect blend of cleverness and nostalgia. It adds an extra layer of depth that rewards longtime fans, turning a simple adaptation into a celebration of Batman's history. This idea could make the series feel unique and buzzworthy.

Getting a major movie star like Christian Bale to commit to an ongoing animated series is extremely unlikely due to budget and schedule. A more realistic choice like Troy Baker might lack the same wow factor, leaving some fans disappointed. The 'gimmick' could also overshadow the actual story.

This reflects a larger trend in modern fiction: self-aware narratives that play with audience expectations. By blurring the line between hero and villain, the casting mirrors the comic's theme that these characters are darker reflections of one another, making the adaptation richer.

If such a casting happens, it could set a new standard for comic adaptations — not just picking voices that fit, but voices that carry symbolic weight. Future projects might also mine actors' old roles to create meta-layers, though they must still deliver a compelling standalone story.
